events.title: One developer against the Swarm: how Kepler Protocol gets developed and tested
events.summary: {STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/46097557/08aee707d9d3bc223de02be8a9ad95ac7f2d47fb.png Kepler Protocol is made without a team: one developer, no test lab, no QA department. Even so, the game is played, checked and measured day and night. Three engines that grew alongside the game make that possible. Three engines instead of a team Setzwerk is the world. events.title: Demo update 0.9.44 — a clear goal, and the swarm comes
events.summary: Thank you for your feedback from Next Fest — many of you told us the goal was unclear and the swarm never showed up. Version 0.9.44 answers both. Everything from 0.9.43 and earlier follows below. Goal — at landing the staff sets you a clear goal: "Establish a bridgehead — survey the Flux core". The hint bar shows it with its three steps and suggests a next step — how you get there is up to you. events.title: Fifteen Weeks on Kepler-186e
events.summary: The demo is here. It ends exactly where the game begins — and that is on purpose.Starting today you can play Kepler Protocol. Not all of it — the first fifteen weeks. The demo is free and waiting on the store page, in time for Steam Next Fest from October 19 to 26.The version number sits in the bottom left of the main menu. events.title: Six out of Twenty-Nine
events.summary: For two devblogs running we promised the same thing: the drill is next. Here it is. It no longer wins on its own — but it no longer loses unnoticed either.{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/46097557/f7c74211caa7f0cee77e895e2298510af290e9ef.pngThe Empire can win on Kepler in three ways. It can hold out for seventy turns until the fortress stands. It can storm the Alpha Nest — get in, strike down the queen, hold for three turns. events.title: The Army Nobody Saw Die
events.summary: We spent a night playing 540 games against ourselves. What we were looking for, we didn't find. What we found was worse.{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/46097557/f184966bf6feeb1eabad8ab5a5e9ffa17b1ef148.pngKepler Protocol isn't only tested by hand. We have a second system that plays the game when nobody is watching: two AI sides, the full rulebook, real maps — and a log that records every turn. events.title: What Falls Does Not Fully Return
events.summary: Across thousands of games no one died in our battles. The casualty counter lied. Not this time.A battle in Kepler Protocol is fought, won or lost, formations break — and afterwards, in the report, a number: the fallen. Across thousands of test games that number read zero. On both sides. Not one soldier who failed to come home. The formations dissolved, but the people in them went nowhere — they had never existed, on paper.It was a silent bug, slipped in during a rebuild of the combat system. The

events.title: The Swarm Matures
events.summary: We have dissected the Swarm once before: how it decides — no commander, only pheromone gradients. Today is about how it grows up. In one test game the Swarm tipped into a war mood after barely two months — the pheromone field glowing, swarms boiling outward, the brood chambers pulsing. An Imperial patrol pushed in, expecting armoured beetles. It found leaping predators. Small, fast, biting things — and nothing else. The heavy legions the Swarm is feared for were not there. events.title: The Core Drill
events.summary: For seventeen thousand games the Kaiserreich's greatest structure never once fired. The drill was not to blame.The planetary core drill is outright victory. A monument of Krupp steel and flux that grinds through the planet's crust into the Swarm's brood chamber — activate it, and Kepler-186e is yours. That is the design. events.title: Ordo Arachnis — Where Command Ends
events.summary: When the enemy has no mind yet still decides. In a test round of Kepler Protocol, an Imperial reconnaissance patrol observed a swarm-pack two fields away. The pack was heading north — direction clear, pace steady. Then, mid-movement, it turned west. No visible cause. No order from anywhere.We searched the log for a directive. There was none. events.title: Mission Command — When the AI Decides Its Own Moves
events.summary: In an early playtest of Kepler Protocol, the Kaiserreich's main army stood in front of Hive Beta. Fully manned, in combat, pinned. Back at the home base: a barracks, a reserve pool of soldiers, the material for a second corps. The AI saw all of it. And did nothing. That was a poor default we'd built ourselves: one brigade per turn when the army had room. If not — standstill. No matter how clear the situation was. We solved it with an old Prussian principle: Auftragstaktik (mission command). Molt
